newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Germany may win Holzmann case back, analysts say.
newsitem.headline: Germany may win Holzmann case back, analysts say.

text.p: Plans by two German construction giants to pool their forces looked likely on Tuesday to set off another dispute between the European Commission and Germany over merger control.
But this time the German Cartel Office may win the fight.

Germany's two largest building firms Philip Holzmann AG and Hochtief AG effectively pooled forces on Tuesday through a deal between Hochtief and Deutsche Bank which gives them joint control of Holzmann.
The Bundeskartellamt German merger authority in Berlin immediately rejected the deal, saying it would ask the Commission to give it responsibility for the case.
The Commission said it would examine th3e German request, the spokesman for European Competition Commissioner Karel Van Miert said.
"If we notice that it's not for us but for the German authorities we'll send it back," he added.
The deal has not been formally notified to the Commission for clearance, but the companies' lawyers have already sounded the EU's competition services, EU sources said.

The key argument in favour of the German request is that the European construction sector is still to a large extent divided along national lines despite EU attempts to control it, notably through European public procurement rules on public works, industry and antitrust lawyers said.

Germany will be using a provision in the EU's merger regulation, which applies to the Holzmann case, allowing national competition authorities to regain jurisdiction over a merger or takeover if it risks harming fair competition in its market.
The key proviso is that the affected national market must be "distinct" from the other European markets.
The Commission itself has indicated in the past that this may be the case.
In February, it cleared the acquisition by Britain's Amec Plc of French giant Spie Batignolles saying notably that "each of the companies operates principally in its own domestic market".
The Commission may also be reluctant to keep for itself a deal which was drafted with the purpose of qualifying for EU review and to escape the German objections.

"If the Commission gets the sense it's being used as a device for escaping the jurisdiction of the Bundeskartellamt it might be more favourably inclined to granting the German request," Alec Burnside, a partner with law firm Linklaters & Paines, said.
Past attempts by Germany to regain control over controversial alliances on the grounds that the affected market was German rather than European have been unsuccessful.
It lost in 1995 over the MSG pay-television deal between Bertelsmann AG, Deutsche Telekom and Leo Kirch which was blocked by the Commission.

The Bundeskartellamt also tried unsuccessfully to keep for itself the 1994 salt and potash merger of BASF's Kali & Salz and east German MDK. The deal was cleared with tough conditions which the companies are still challenging in the European court.

Although agreeing in both cases that Germany was the most affected market, the Commission took the view that Kali Salz operated in a European market and that the European media market was set to expand.
